analysis.one_liner: Lets union contracts require workers to pay union dues, overriding state right-to-work laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a floor vote: it was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and died when the 116th Congress ended, with 32 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the section of federal labor law that lets states pass "right-to-work" laws. Today, more than half the states use that authority to ban union contracts that require workers to join the union or pay dues as a condition of their job. This bill would erase that state option nationwide, so unions could negotiate such agreements anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who want union representation in right-to-work states, and the unions that represent them. When a union contract covers workers who cannot be forced to pay, "free riders" get the benefits without paying the cost, which starves unions of dues. Repealing the state option lets unions collect dues from everyone covered by a contract, giving them a stable budget for bargaining, grievance handling, and organizing — and stronger unions have historically won higher wages and better benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers seeking unions in right-to-work states

how_it_helps.text: Repeals Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act, the provision that lets states ban union security agreements, so federal law would once again allow contracts requiring union membership or dues as a condition of employment in every state.

This fixes the free-rider problem: under right-to-work rules, workers covered by a union contract can take the higher wages and contract protections without paying dues, which weakens the union's ability to negotiate and enforce the contract for everyone.

A stable dues base in right-to-work states would give unions more resources for bargaining, which union workers have historically used to win higher pay and better working conditions than comparable non-union workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers in right-to-work states would face stronger unions with steadier funding, likely leading to higher labor costs and less unilateral control over workplace rules. Some workers in those states who prefer not to join or fund a union would lose that choice: where a union negotiates a security agreement, paying dues or an agency fee would become a condition of the job.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers in right-to-work states; some workers

drawbacks.text: Workers in right-to-work states who do not want to belong to or pay for a union would lose that option: once a union and employer negotiate a union security agreement, paying dues or fees would be a condition of employment, which many see as forced political and financial association.
The bill overrides the choices of state legislatures and voters in the more than half of states that have adopted right-to-work laws, removing a policy decision those states have made for themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who want collective bargaining, the bill removes a major structural obstacle — right-to-work rules let workers take contract benefits without paying, which drains unions over time. The honest cost falls on two groups: employers, who would face better-funded unions and higher labor costs, and the minority of workers who genuinely prefer not to fund a union and would no longer be able to opt out where a union security agreement exists. Whether that trade is worth it depends on how much you weight collective worker power against individual choice; the bill does not attempt a middle ground and simply preempts state law entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on January 29, 2020, joined by 31 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
That same day it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor, which took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

The bill ended the Congress with 32 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no companion movement in the Senate; it never came up for a vote in either chamber and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in right-to-work states keep the weaker, dues-starved unions that the status quo gives them, and workers who prefer not to pay dues keep that option. The bill's supporters — unions and pro-union workers — got nothing.

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the federal provision allowing state right-to-work laws.

for.name: 32 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no further action on the bill occurred.

against.name: Bobby Scott
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after it was referred to his committee; it received no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: 197 of 197 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Not one member signed on as a cosponsor.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all 32 cosponsors were House Democrats, no Republican ever signed on, and the bill never reached a vote in either chamber.

industries.note: Unions could negotiate union security agreements in right-to-work states, ending the free-rider problem and giving them a stable dues base for bargaining and organizing. Since unions are organizations of the workers themselves, their gain runs largely alongside the interests of workers who want collective representation.

Employers in right-to-work states currently bargain with unions that cannot require dues payments, which keeps union finances thin and bargaining power limited. The bill would let unions charge every covered worker, raising labor costs and strengthening the union side of the table.
